messages.author: e19ea506112fd25b
messages.subject: random effect modeling
parts:
Hi,

I am looking for an advice on random effect modeling. Although from physical perspective it makes sense to put random effect on some parameters perhaps it is not computationally feasible to handle the cases when those parameters are multiplied. By taking simple simple harmonic oscillator example:
functions {
  real[] sho(real t,real[] y,real[] theta,real[] x_r,int[] x_i) {
    real dydt[2];
    dydt[1] = y[2];
    dydt[2] = -y[1] - theta[1] * y[2];
    return dydt;
  }
}
and modifying it slightly:
functions {
  real[] sho(real t,real[] y,real[] theta,real[] x_r,int[] x_i) {
    real dydt[2];
    dydt[1] = y[2] + theta[1];
    dydt[2] = -y[1] - theta[1] * theta[2] * y[2];
    return dydt;
  }
}
Is it OK to put random effects on both thetas? What tricks can be used to prevent nonidentifiability?

Actual code is attached. Actual question is if I can put random effects on Kpu_scale and Kid_Vmax at the same time. Those parameters are expected to vary from individual to individual but if it leads to nonidentifiability I have to find a work around.
      ydot[32+1] = (CL_glom*y[6+1]*Kpu_scale/0.760023139372961*1+y[6+1]*Kpu_scale/0.760023139372961*1*Kid_Vmax/(y[6+1]*Kpu_scale/0.760023139372961+Kid_Km));


Thanks for any insight,
Linas

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] random effect modeling
parts:
It only makes sense to have random effects if there's enough data
to get information out of the fit. So yes, you can put random effects
on everything.

If they have different priors and are used in different instances,
you can still fit with multiplications, though it's not ideal
for identifiability, either statistically or computationally.

- Bob
